segments.text: This experiment compares SHA-3-256 in the compact core with oxide's quartz implementation.
The input comes from block RAM, memory built into the FPGA.
That lets the comparison focus on the hardware hashing path.
A small, repeatable pattern is loaded once.
The FPGA reads it, returns to the beginning, and keeps the stream moving.
The hash state continues across every pass.
A small memory can therefore supply one large continuous message.
The hardware timer starts with the hash job and stops when the digest is ready.
Loading the pattern happens before timing begins.
The measurement includes the memory reader, framing, and the selected hash core.
Both cores use the same board, the same memory path, and a 100 MHz clock.
Messages start at 64 bytes and double at each step, across 25 sizes.
7 measured runs follow warmup at every size. That's 350 measured hashes in this replay
experiment.
Now follow the throughput as the messages grow. Oxide's quartz settles at about 100 megabytes
per second. The compact core reaches 238.6. Once the messages are large, both curves
settle into a steady rate.
The speedup is quartz's time divided by the compact core's time. 1 means equal speed.
speed. For large messages, the Compact Core settles at about 2.39 times the throughput.
Its advantage stays there as the message keeps growing.
For the largest message, about 1,074 megabytes, Quartz takes 10.737 seconds. The Compact
Core takes 4.5. The input is identical. Both implementations produce the same digest.
The compact hash partition also uses fewer resources, 21.9% fewer lookup tables, and about 58% fewer flip-flops.
The replay memory is shared infrastructure, counted separately from those hash partition totals.
Credit to Oxide and the Quartz contributors for the reference core.
Their unchanged source and license are retained alongside the measurements and scripts.
